questions.prompt: A feature is code-complete and the team wants it in front of learners this week.

items.text: Run the unit and instrumented suites against the release variant
Push the build to the internal testing track
Watch crash-free rate and ANR before widening the rollout

questions.explanation: Test the artifact you're actually shipping — release builds differ from debug by minification alone, and R8 breaks reflection-based code that debug builds never notice. Internal track first, then a staged rollout, because a 10% rollout you can halt is the only real safety net Play gives you. Watching the metrics is what makes the stage meaningful; skipping it makes it theatre.

questions.prompt: Crash-free users sits at 99.6%, but Play Console is warning about a 1.2% ANR rate. What is it telling you?
options: ANRs are just crashes on older devices — same root causes.
The app is being killed for using too much memory.
The main thread was blocked long enough for the system to offer to kill the app. Look for I/O or heavy work on the main thread, very often during startup.
ANRs only come from background services and can be ignored for a UI app.
questions.explanation: ANRs and crashes are different failures with different fixes: a crash is code that threw, an ANR is code that wouldn't yield. They also hurt differently — ANR rate feeds Play's quality thresholds and can suppress your store ranking while your crash numbers look excellent.

questions.prompt: Cold start went from 1.2s to 2.4s in one release. On a modularised app, where do you look?
options: Something moved into Application.onCreate or a startup content provider — usually a library initialising eagerly.
Too many modules — module count slows startup.
Compose is slow to start up.
questions.explanation: Cold start regressions are nearly always eager initialisation: an analytics or crash SDK added to onCreate, or a library that installs its own ContentProvider and runs before your code does. App Startup lets you make those lazy. Module count affects build time, not runtime.

questions.prompt: Crash-free users look healthy after a release, but support reports that many users cannot complete checkout. What metric assumption is dangerous?

subject.content: Crash-free is above 99.9%, so the release is healthy.

options: Crash-free users should be measured hourly only.
A non-crashing functional failure can destroy a critical journey while crash metrics stay green; release health also needs journey success, ANR, latency, and business signals.
Support tickets should never influence release decisions.
The staged rollout should immediately move to 100%.
questions.explanation: Crash-free rate measures one failure mode. A release can remain perfectly stable while a server response, feature flag, or UI state prevents payment. Health criteria must include the user journeys the release can break.
